query: Why do some agents have longer resolution times?

per_column.name: assigned_agent
per_column.rationale: The query asks why some AGENTS have longer resolution times; the agent identity is the candidate cause whose effect on resolution time is being attributed. It is explicitly named in the query.

per_column.name: incident_category
per_column.rationale: Category (e.g., email_server vs vpn) plausibly drives which agents get assigned (routing/specialization) and independently affects resolution time. A genuine common cause of both treatment and outcome, surfaced from data, not named in query.

per_column.name: issue_complexity
per_column.rationale: Complexity can influence assignment (harder tickets routed to certain agents) and directly lengthens resolution time. A common cause of both; not named in query.

per_column.name: incident_severity_proxy
per_column.rationale: Severity/impact affects who is assigned (escalation to senior agents) and the effort/time to resolve. Plausible common cause of treatment and outcome; not named in query.

per_column.name: resolution_mechanism
per_column.rationale: The required fix (server_restart, credentials_reset, etc.) lies on the causal path between the agent's handling/incident and the resolution time; it is a consequence of how the ticket is worked, so it is a mediator, not a confounder. Adjusting for it would be a mistake.

judge.rationale: The columns set up a genuine causal estimation: assigned_agent is the treatment (named in query), and the outcome is resolution time. Three confounders (category, complexity, severity_proxy) are plausible common causes of both agent assignment and resolution time, and none were named in the query, demonstrating real surfacing of confounders. resolution_mechanism is a mediator, not a confounder, so it should not be adjusted for. Overall this is a strong instance of causal attribution with novel confounders, slightly discounted for including a mediator alongside the confounders.
